extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys) engaged in patent prosecution
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and presenting secondary considerations (unexpected results, commercial success, long‑felt need, copying, skepticism, etc.) in support of nonobviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 during patent examination and prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected results — commensurate in scope with claimed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The objective evidence of nonobviousness must be commensurate in scope with the claims which the evidence is offered to support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether unexpected results are unexpectedly improved results or a property not taught by the prior art, the showing must be reviewed to see if the results occur over the entire claimed range. If the evidence is limited to a narrow species or narrow conditions, it may be insufficient to rebut a prima facie case for broader claims (citing In re Clemens; In re Grasselli).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of species or narrower-range data to support a genus or broader claimed range
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonobviousness of a genus or claimed range may be supported by data showing unexpected results of a species or narrower range under certain circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A broader claimed range can be supported if one of ordinary skill can determine a trend in the exemplified data allowing reasonable extension of probative value. Limited species testing may be inadequate if it does not provide basis to conclude similar results across the generic scope (citing In re Kollman; In re Lindner).

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrating criticality of a claimed range
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish unexpected results over a claimed range, applicants should compare a sufficient number of tests both inside and outside the claimed range to show the criticality of the claimed range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative testing should be sufficient in amount and scope to demonstrate criticality; courts have reversed or affirmed based on whether tests were commensurate with claim scope (citing In re Hill).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison with the closest prior art (affidavit/declaration requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 must compare the claimed subject matter with the closest prior art to be effective to rebut a prima facie case of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare claimed invention with disclosure of each cited reference to determine number and importance of common limitations. Deviations from reference disclosures should be explained and evaluated; applicants may compare against prior art closer than the examiner relied upon. Where there are two equally close references, unexpected results over only one will not rebut obviousness unless teachings are sufficiently similar so testing one informs about the other (citing In re Burckel; In re Merchant; In re Holladay; Ex parte Humber; In re Johnson; In re Payne). Applicant is not required to compare to non‑existent prior art suggested by combinations of references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages disclosed or inherent (totality of the record)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence and arguments directed to advantages not disclosed in the specification cannot be disregarded; obviousness is determined by the totality of the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants' evidence or arguments traversing a § 103 rejection need not be contained within the specification. Undisclosed advantages that inherently flow from disclosed uses should be considered. The specification need not disclose proportions or values as critical for applicants to present evidence showing proportions/values to be critical (citing In re Chu; In re Zenitz; Ex parte Sasajima; In re Saunders).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of declarations and affidavits (37 CFR 1.132) — reliability requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Declarations or affidavits are required to obtain assurances that statements or representations made are correct; publications should not substitute for expert testimony that the statute contemplates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publications may be considered to the extent probative, but the reason for requiring declaration/affidavit form is statutory assurances (citing Ex parte Gray). Declarations must meet the statutory form and cannot be casually substituted by publications when testimony is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nexus between claimed invention and commercial success (burden of proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant asserting commercial success to support nonobviousness bears the burden of proof of establishing a nexus between the claimed invention and the evidence of commercial success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'nexus' designates a factually and legally sufficient connection so the evidence is probative. The PTO must rely on the applicant to provide hard evidence of commercial success; showing commercial success of articles not covered by the claims is not probative (citing In re Huang; In re GPAC; In re Paulsen; Ex parte Remark). Commercial success abroad is relevant as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success must be commensurate in scope with the claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence of commercial success must be commensurate in scope with the claims; commercial success must be due to claimed features, not unclaimed features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of success of a product broader or narrower than the claims may be insufficient. An affidavit stating sales of a product 'constructed according to the disclosure and claims' is not enough because it lacks proof the sold product corresponds to the claimed invention. If the commercial product is not coextensive with the claimed invention, applicants must show a legally sufficient relationship between the claimed feature and the commercial product/process (citing In re Tiffin; Joy Technologies; In re Hollingsworth; Demaco).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success must be derived from the claimed invention (not extraneous business factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial success must flow from the functions and advantages disclosed or inherent in the specification and not from promotion, advertising, brand recognition, or other business events extraneous to the merits of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must determine success is directly derived from claimed features in a marketplace where consumers choose on objective principles. Conclusory inventor opinions are insufficient to show nexus. Licensing evidence must be carefully appraised because licensing can succeed for reasons unrelated to invention merits. In design patents, establishing nexus is especially difficult because sales may be due to brand or performance rather than design (citing In re Mageli; In re Noznick; Demaco; Pentec; Hybritech; Litton Systems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sales figures and market evidence must be adequately defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Gross sales figures alone do not establish commercial success absent contextual evidence such as market share, time period of sales, or what sales would normally be expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide market share data, duration of sales, and baseline expectations for the market to make gross sales meaningful. Without this context, sales figures are of little probative value (citing Cable Electric; Ex parte Standish).

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-felt need and failure of others
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed invention must satisfy a long‑felt need which was recognized, persistent, and not solved by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish objective evidence that a recognized problem existed for a long period without solution. The need must have been recognized by those skilled in the art and not satisfied by prior products. Long‑felt need is measured from the date the problem is identified and efforts are made to solve it. Consider other factors (lack of interest, lack of appreciation of potential/marketability) that might explain failure of others (citing In re Gershon; Orthopedic Equipment; Newell; In re Cavanagh; Texas Instruments; Scully Signal; Environmental Designs; In re Tiffin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism of experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions of disbelief by experts constitute strong evidence of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skepticism expressed before inventors proved experts wrong is entitled to fair evidentiary weight; multi‑year research preceding an invention can support nonobviousness. Testimony of initial incredulity and skepticism may rebut a prima facie case of obviousness (citing Environmental Designs; In re Dow Chemical; Burlington Industries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Copying by competitors as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that competitors are copying the invention can be presented as secondary evidence of nonobviousness, but more than mere copying is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copying is persuasive where an alleged infringer tried for a substantial time to design a similar product and failed, then copied. Copying is not persuasive where the copy is not identical or the competitor had not expended significant effort to develop its own solution (citing Cable Electric; Dow Chemical; Pentec; Vandenberg; Panduit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inoperability of references (burden to rebut presumption)
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits or declarations attacking the operability of a patent cited as a reference must rebut the presumption of operability by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should not casually opine on operability because patents are presumed operable. Mere showing that one can operate within a disclosure without obtaining the alleged product does not overcome the presumption that a skilled artisan, making routine experiments/adaptations, would achieve the disclosed result. Failures by experimenters with no interest in succeeding carry less weight. If inoperability is asserted only for features not relied upon, the reference remains effective for operative features. Patentee declarations that they did not intend the disclosure to be used as claimed are immaterial (citing Metropolitan Eng.; In re Sasse; In re Weber; In re Michalek; In re Reid; In re Shepherd; In re Crosby; In re Epstein; In re Pio; In re Yale).

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility and operability of applicant's disclosure (when to require evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on when it is proper to require evidence of utility or operativeness and how to evaluate evidence submitted to overcome a 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2107.01 and § 2107 - § 2107.02 for detailed precedent and evaluation approaches. Examiners should understand circumstances that justify requiring evidence and how to weigh it relative to statutory utility/operability requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of disclosure (enablement) — applicant burden after prima facie showing
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the examiner establishes a prima facie case of lack of enablement under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, the burden falls on the applicant to present persuasive arguments supported by suitable proofs where necessary that one skilled in the art could make and use the claimed invention using the disclosure as a guide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits or declarations cannot be used to establish facts the specification should recite. Evidence supplementing a deficient specification must show the information to be read into the specification was known to those skilled in the art. Opinion testimony merely asserting disclosure exists is given little weight; testimony that explains underlying factual basis may be admitted and weighed on a case-by-case basis (citing In re Brandstadter; In re Howarth; In re Buchner; In re Smyth; In re Oppenauer; Glaser v. Strickland).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution affidavits/declarations (R-1) to overcome references
rubrics_metrics.description: Under certain circumstances an affidavit or declaration may be submitted to attribute a reference or part of a reference to the applicant, thereby removing the reference as prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If successful, the reference is no longer applicable. For example, if a joint patent discloses subject matter later claimed by S, a 1.132 affidavit may show prior invention by S. Where published articles or patents identify authorship/inventorship, designation does not create a presumption of inventorship; applicants must provide a satisfactory showing that the reference-derived subject matter originated with applicant. An uncontradicted unequivocal statement by applicant may be accepted, but may be insufficient where contrary evidence exists. A successful 1.132 affidavit does not change publication dates for other references (citing In re Katz; In re DeBaun; Ex parte Kroger; In re Carreira; In re Costello).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disqualifying a commonly owned patent as prior art (37 CFR 1.130 requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 relies on a U.S. patent not prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(b) and the inventions are commonly owned and not patentably distinct, the applicant/owner may disqualify the patent as prior art by complying with 37 CFR 1.130.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patent can be disqualified as prior art by submission of: (1) a terminal disclaimer under § 1.321(c), and (2) an oath or declaration that the application/patent and the patent are currently owned by the same party and that the inventor named is the prior inventor under 35 U.S.C. 104. (See 37 CFR 1.130(a).)
